deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Uncapped CAM in Medical Leases

For medical practices, the Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clause is often the most significant source of financial volatility in a commercial lease. Landlords frequently draft these provisions with broad, "all-encompassing" language designed to pass through virtually any cost associated with the property's operation. The danger lies in the lack of distinction between routine, day-to-day maintenance and significant, long-term capital expenditures.

An unscrupulous landlord may attempt to categorize a full parking lot resurfacing, a roof replacement, or a complete HVAC system overhaul as a "maintenance expense." Because medical tenants often rely on highly predictable overhead to manage patient care, specialized staffing, and expensive medical equipment, these sudden, massive spikes in CAM charges can jeopardize the practice's solvency. Furthermore, without a clear definition of "controllable" expenses, you may find yourself subsidizing the landlord's administrative inefficiencies, increased security for other tenants, or even the costs of upgrading the building's amenities for new, higher-paying tenants.

Strategic Protections and Expense Caps

To protect your practice, you must move beyond simple acceptance of the landlord's standard form. A sophisticated lease negotiation focuses on two primary levers: the exclusion of capital improvements and the implementation of an annual cap on controllable expenses. The goal is to transform an unpredictable variable cost into a manageable, predictable line item in your operating budget.

  • Exclusion of Capital Improvements: Ensure that any structural repairs or replacements that provide long-term value to the landlord are explicitly excluded from the CAM pool. If the landlord insists on passing these through, ensure they are amortized over their useful life and only charged during your lease term.
  • Controllable Expense Caps: Negotiate a "cap" (typically between 3% and 5%) on expenses that the landlord can influence, such as landscaping, janitorial services, and management fees.
  • Audit Rights: Secure the right to audit the landlord's books and records annually to verify that the CAM charges are being calculated accurately and in accordance with the lease terms.
  • Definition of Operating Expenses: Narrow the scope of "operating expenses" to exclude administrative overhead, legal fees related to other tenants, and marketing costs for the building.
  • Sanitation Specifics: For medical tenants, ensure that specialized cleaning requirements are clearly defined so you are not billed for general building cleaning that does not meet your clinical standards.

Navigating these technicalities requires an eagle eye for linguistic loopholes and a deep understanding of property management accounting.
